    Bringing Your Citrus Trees Indoors for Winter? Get These 6 Things Right to Avoid Leaf Drop and Pests

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun.
    • Recent findings suggest that the move itself is a shock, though.
    • It has been revealed that that goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun. Then the cold arrives. Citrus can't take a hard freeze, so in colder climates, potted trees have to come inside for winter.

    Recent findings suggest that the move itself is a shock, though. Gardeners who try growing citrus indoors often find a scatter of leaves on the floor soon after. Indoor light is weaker, the air is drier, and pests that rode in on the branches can spread to nearby houseplants.

    It has been revealed that that goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike. Six checks before the tree comes through the door can head off much of that.

    Recent findings suggest that most citrus can be damaged below 32°F (0°C), and a potted tree is more exposed than one in the ground. Lemons and limes are usually the most tender, while kumquats, satsumas, and calamondins can handle a little more chill. Aim to have the tree inside before nights start dipping into the 40s (4–9°C). Wait for the first freeze warning, and you'll be dragging a heavy pot from full sun straight indoors. Give it a week or two in a shady spot near the house first instead – it adjusts to lower light that way.

    In a recent development, flip the leaves over and look along the midvein. Brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum) shows up there as small, flat, tan bumps. Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) leave pale speckles and, eventually, fine webbing where the leaf meets the stem, and white, cottony clumps in the leaf joints usually mean citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri).

    If you find anything, spray the tree outdoors with an insecticidal soap or a horticultural oil labeled for citrus, such as Monterey horticultural oil concentrate. Plan on more than one round. Once inside, keep it away from other houseplants for three or four weeks.

    Bugs don't only ride in on the leaves. Tip the pot on its side, look in the drainage holes, and lift the saucer. Slugs, sowbugs, and earwigs all like that damp spot underneath, and ants sometimes leave small piles of potting mix they've hauled out. A slow soak with the hose drives many of them out.

    Recent findings suggest that check any roots poking through the holes, too. Firm, light-colored roots are a good sign, but dark, mushy ones and a sour smell point to waterlogged soil. Unless the roots are in real trouble, wait to repot citrus trees until spring.

    Citrus needs far more light than a pothos or snake plant. Indoors, aim for at least six hours of bright light a day. A south- or southwest-facing window is usually the best spot, with the tree close to the glass but not touching it. Up north, short winter days often fall short – that's when a grow light helps. Glowrium sells a dual-head LED grow light on Amazon that's just under 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, with heads that bend toward the canopy. Trees moved from full sun to a dim corner overnight often shed a good share of their leaves.

    Hold a hand over a heating vent or radiator when the heat kicks on. That hot, dry air blows straight across the leaves of a nearby tree, and a cold, drafty window or door is no better. Sudden swings like those commonly trigger leaf drop. Somewhere around 65–75°F (18–24°C) by day and a little cooler at night, about 55–65°F (13–18°C), works well.

    Humidity near 50% helps in a heated house. The Pure Enrichment MistAire humidifier from Walmart runs up to 25 hours on a tank, and the ThermoPro digital hygrometer can sit by the pot to track both.

    It has been revealed that on a hot patio, potted citrus can need water every day or two. Indoors, with cooler rooms and less light, it uses much less, and the summer routine can drown the roots. Push a finger about 2 inches (5 cm) into the mix, and water only when it feels dry at that depth. Deep pots are harder to judge, which is where a moisture meter, like the Xlux Long Probe Plant Soil Moisture Meter, is invaluable.

    Industry observers note that water until some drains out, then empty the saucer. Set the pot on a few terra-cotta Pot Toes to keep the drainage holes clear. Don't overcorrect, though – a tree left bone dry for long stretches drops flowers and can lose leaves.

    Some leaf drop in the first few weeks is common. Less light, drier air, and new temperatures all hit at once, and a few leaves on the floor are just part of it, mostly.

    Sources indicate that look closer if leaves keep falling after the first month or whole branches go bare. A wet, sour-smelling mix points to overwatering, while a mix that's dry all the way down means it went too long between drinks. Check how close the tree sits to a vent or cold door, and whether that window is as bright in December as it seemed in October. Sticky spots, webbing, or cottony clumps under the leaves mean pests got past the quarantine.

    According to recent reports, get through those six checks, and your tree has an easier winter ahead. Come spring, once nights stay above 50°F (10°C), it can head back out to the patio a little at a time.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success demonstrates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is presently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in Upcoming York City on behalf of ISIS.

    It has been revealed that “Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in Newly introduced York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”.

    “We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” stated U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”.

    “Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”.

    Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

    Sources indicate that the first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

    At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in Latest York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

    An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the Latest York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

    This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.

    It has been revealed that assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

    When my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

    Recent findings suggest that itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

    Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

    According to recent reports, you have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

    I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

    Sources indicate that please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

    It has been revealed that I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical concerns sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

    He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

    This Banana Bag Trick Triggers a Christmas Cactus to Bloom – Try it if You Don't See Buds By November

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that if your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective.
    • Pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones.
    • We all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that if your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective. It’s so disappointing when a Schlumbergera isn’t showing even the smallest pinpricks of colored buds on its stem ends by late fall, especially if you’ve been diligently delivering all the care your Christmas cactus needs in November. But by shifting your stubborn plant into survival mode, you can kickstart its bloom cycle. And guess what? All you need is a banana and a plastic bag.

    Pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones. This causes the plants to stop growing green leaf segments and switch to developing flowerbuds. And you can use the exact same idea with the natural chemicals a ripe banana releases if your Christmas cactus isn't blooming yet.

    We all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast. That’s down to the ethylene it emits, a natural hormone that plants release when nearing the end of their life cycle. So, by trapping ethylene around your Christmas cactus for a short time, you can trick the plant into thinking it’s under extreme threat, which triggers it to develop flowers as a last-ditch survival effort to preserve its genetics via seed production. Clever, huh?

    In a recent development, highly ripe bananas that have brown spots or are turning brown emit the highest levels of ethylene. You only need to use the peel: though the whole fruit produces ethylene gas, the soft, sweet flesh of a banana is a magnet for fruit flies and fungus gnats and adds too much moisture to the little greenhouse you’re about to create.

    Excess moisture will quickly evaporate from the inner surface of the peel, further reducing humidity and any risk of pests or disease.

    Now stand your Christmas cactus, still in its container, on a plate or significant plant saucer and lay the banana peel alongside the pot base. It’s important that the peel doesn’t touch the leaf segments or soil as this risks transferring mold or fungal spores.

    Pull a clear plastic bag down over the plant, plate and banana peel, and tuck or tie under the plate to seal. If the bag is flimsy and falls onto the stems, use chopsticks or skewers poked into the soil to create a frame so there's no direction contact between plant and plastic.

    Sources indicate that it’s vital the bag is clear as an opaque bag is likely to take the stress a step too far and your plant may drop leaf segments instead of developing buds. It also means you can keep a close eye on your plant through the process. A clear unscented trash bag like this from Amazon is ideal as it's plenty big enough to make fashioning your mini-greenhouse easy.

    Now your Christmas cactus is in its little greenhouse, it’ll quickly overheat if it’s hit by the sun’s rays so find it a spot in a bright room but out of direct sunlight.

    The optimum amount of time to leave your Schlumbergera in its ethylene tank is exactly 2 days and 2 nights. This gives the gas plenty of time to chemically shock the plant and trigger bud development, without damaging the plant or giving mold a chance to develop in the restricted air circulation.

    While professional growers use incredibly precise parts-per-million doses of synthetic chemicals, you can’t tell exactly how much ethylene your chosen banana is emitting. So, keep an eye on your Christmas cactus and if at any point the plant looks like it’s struggling or there’s the slightest sign of mold, remove the bag straight away. Don’t be tempted to leave the bag on any longer than 48 hours as too much ethylene can harm bud development.

    Recent findings suggest that carefully take off the plastic bag, discard the peel and place your plant in the spot where you want it to flower, being sure to avoid these Christmas cactus disaster zones. After a week or so, you should see pinhead-sized bumps starting to form on the leaf segment tips and by two weeks, they should be clearly visible.

    According to recent reports, it’s vital you check your plant hasn’t already begun developing buds before trying this trick. Inspect leaf tips under a bright light – or use a cheap magnifying glass with LED light like this from Amazon – to look for any bumps beginning to form right on the tips of the leaf segments. These may be tiny so gently feel for them with a fingertip, too. If your Schlumbergera has pink or red flowers these little bumps will be bright but if your plant blooms white they may be green and harder to spot.

    If you’re in any doubt, wait a week and see if those bumps get any bigger. While using ethylene from ripe banana peel is a very effective way to get a Christmas cactus to flower, this hormone shock can also cause existing buds to stall if the process has already begun.

    If this pro growers' trick doesn’t work, there’s likely an underlying reason why your Christmas cactus isn't flowering, that’s overriding the plant’s system.

    Sources indicate that the banana bag trick is well worth trying if your Christmas cactus doesn’t have buds yet, and you still just have enough time to trigger your plant into producing flowers for the holidays. Next year, be sure to use the black-out hack that tricks your Christmas cactus into flowering right on time, and you won’t have to worry!

    • What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

    It has been revealed that that is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is at the moment looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

    This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

    In a recent development, TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

    Rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

    The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

    It has been revealed that the Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

    For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

    Industry observers note that lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

    Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

    TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

    The current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

    Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

    Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

    Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

    Sources indicate that for families who decide to participate, it is vital to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

    When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

    Industry observers note that the recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

    There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a big deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

    In a recent development, but this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

    Aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

    The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

    Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

    The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

    Recent findings suggest that itâs important to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

    When it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

    And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

    According to recent reports, that's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

    For owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

    So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

    • The Department of Justice and FBI revealed today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Department of Justice and FBI revealed today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

    In a recent development, in its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered. FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations. Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

    According to recent reports, “The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”.

    “This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” mentioned FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

    Sources indicate that “Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” noted Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”.

    Industry observers note that “Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come.".

    Examples of cases charged during this period include:.

    In the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses. Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted. In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

    In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

    Sources indicate that in the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

    In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo. His case is pending trial.

    Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

    In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

    FBI’s Operation Steadfast Promise.

    Sources indicate that operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

    This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

    During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

    Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a new FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

    Industry observers note that the FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

    The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

    Industry observers note that halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

    Halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

    Industry observers note that keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

    Recent findings suggest that costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs notable to pay attention to how they respond.

    A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

    Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

    A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

    Industry observers note that there's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

    Recent findings suggest that halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

    It has been revealed that A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

    Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

    Recent findings suggest that jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

    Real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

    Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

    The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

    Sources indicate that check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

    Recent findings suggest that handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

    It has been revealed that closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

    Keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

    An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly vital on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

    Sources indicate that if a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

    In a recent development, check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

    Recent findings suggest that halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

    It has been revealed that it's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When you think of a Christmas tree, chances are you picture a familiar fir or spruce, perhaps decorated with twinkling lights and festive ornaments. But, for some people, Christmas looks a little different.

    That's right; instead of bringing an evergreen indoors, many people celebrate the season beneath a spectacular flowering tree covered in brilliant red blooms. Meet the New Zealand Christmas Tree, also known as the pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa). This extraordinary evergreen puts on one of the most eye-catching floral displays of summer, transforming coastlines and gardens with masses of vibrant crimson flowers.

    And while it might not be the easiest Christmas tree for gardeners in the US to get their hands on, there are some beautiful alternatives that can bring a similar combination of colorful flowers and evergreen foliage to your own outdoor space...

    Shop Flowering Christmas Trees:.

    Recent findings suggest that native to Upcoming Zealand, the pōhutukawa has earned its festive nickname thanks to its spectacular flowering season, which coincides with Christmas in the Southern Hemisphere. Because, while much of the northern hemisphere is welcoming winter with bare branches and chilly temperatures, New Zealand is enjoying the height of summer... and that's when this remarkable tree really comes into its own.

    Rather than having conventional petals, its unmistakable flowers look just like fluffy red brushes (which pollinators love). And, against the tree's glossy green leaves, the effect is nothing short of spectacular.

    A post shared by Hahana (@hahana_official).

    Although it can reach around 65 feet tall in its natural habitat, younger New Zealand Christmas trees can be grown from seed in large containers (although they need plenty of sunshine, well-drained soil and protection from frost).

    Industry observers note that for US gardeners, growing one outdoors will generally be limited to warmer and frost-free USDA Zones, so it isn't necessarily a practical choice for everyone. Luckily, though, there are other flowering evergreens that can deliver a similarly spectacular effect...

    According to recent reports, if it's the striking crimson display of the pōhutukawa that catches your eye, bottlebrush is perhaps the closest alternative when it comes to finding a flowering evergreen that might serve well as a Christmas tree. Especially as its bright red blooms have plenty in common with the Kiwi native.

    According to recent reports, depending on the variety and climate, bottlebrush (available at Walmart) can flower from spring into summer, attracting hummingbirds and other pollinators to the garden. Many varieties are evergreen and container-friendly, too, although they prefer a sunny position and well-drained soil.

    For gardeners who love the idea of a flowering Christmas tree, but prefer something with more traditional-looking blooms, southern magnolia is a beautiful option, as its enormous (and fabulously fragranced) flowers can measure up to 12 inches across.

    In a recent development, while it doesn't have the bright red flowers of the pōhutukawa, it shares some of its most appealing qualities: year-round evergreen foliage, a substantial tree-like presence and an impressive summer floral display. For smaller spaces, consider a compact cultivar such as this 'Little Gem' from Expert Gardener. It has a naturally narrower growth habit than many full-sized southern magnolias, making it a more manageable choice for smaller gardens.

    It can also be grown in a large container so long as you treat it to sufficient room, good drainage and consistent moisture.

    If fragrance is just as important as appearance, gardenia is another gorgeous Christmas tree alternative thanks to its deep-green foliage and exquisite white flowers.

    Recent findings suggest that oh sure, their blooms may be smaller than those of the southern magnolia, but they more than make up for it with their intoxicating perfume. And, as they don't naturally grow into large trees, standard-trained gardenias can make particularly attractive container garden options; generally best suited to warmer USDA growing zones, growing them in pots makes it easier to protect them from cold weather.

    Something like the Frost Proof Gardenia from Nature Hills is happily able to handle temperatures down to 0-10°F, too!

    The New Zealand Christmas Tree is a wonderful reminder that evergreens don't have to be all about foliage; indeed, some of the most spectacular trees and shrubs combine year-round greenery with extraordinary seasonal flowers.

    Whether you choose the fiery red blooms of bottlebrush, the impressive flowers of southern magnolia or the beautiful fragrance of gardenia, there's no shortage of ways to bring that flowering-evergreen look into your own garden. And who knows? You might even find yourself looking at your Christmas tree traditions a little differently as a result...

She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

    Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

    At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

    At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

    Some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

    When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

    âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â.

    Recent findings suggest that mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own crucial role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

    In a recent development, different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

    According to recent reports, that Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

    During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

    At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

    Industry observers note that when a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

    From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

    The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

    Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

    Sources indicate that in 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

    Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

    According to recent reports, spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

    Sources indicate that âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark noted. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â.

    It is a sweet story, but it also shows why understanding each dog's personality matters.

    Hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She notes the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â.

    Camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

    It has been revealed that three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how promptly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

    Sources indicate that two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

    As for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her new home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

    âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â.

    Some dogs find their people promptly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

    Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:.

    âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â.

    Industry observers note that the sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

    Industry observers note that at Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

    Maybe that is what makes them lucky.

    Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

    And that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

    And every morning, people arrive.

    Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

    And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

    Sources indicate that “Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” stated U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”.

    “This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”.

    According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

    Sources indicate that through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

    Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

    Industry observers note that the jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

    HHS-OIG and FBI investigated the case.

    According to recent reports, trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

    On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

    The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that november is peak time for spider mite infestations in houseplants, and the symptoms can easily be mistaken for dust settling on leaves.
    • As soon as we start heating our homes in fall, warm, dry air creates optimum conditions for spider mites to thrive.
    • Spider mites feed on leaves and, left unchecked, can cause significant damage, and readily spread to other houseplants, too.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that november is peak time for spider mite infestations in houseplants, and the symptoms can easily be mistaken for dust settling on leaves. While spider mites can target any houseplant, prayer plants are the most commonly affected, with monstera and alocasia close behind. So, if you're disappointed to discover some houseplant leaves fading, looking dusty or appearing speckled with tiny spots at this time of year, don’t presume it's just dust: check to see if your houseplant has spider mites straight away.

    As soon as we start heating our homes in fall, warm, dry air creates optimum conditions for spider mites to thrive. The time it takes for these pests to reproduce reduces as temperatures rise, and in cozy conditions a single spider mite can turn into a thousand in a couple of weeks. Which is why, when mid-November arrives, numbers suddenly explode and we start spotting spider-mite infestations in houseplants.

    Spider mites feed on leaves and, left unchecked, can cause significant damage, and readily spread to other houseplants, too. These common houseplant pests can be easily managed, though, and the earlier you catch the problem, the easier it is to deal with. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a spider mite infestation.

    First, rule out dust by wiping the houseplant's leaves with a soft, damp cloth. Then look for these signs that signal you could be dealing with a spider mite infestation:.

    According to recent reports, spider mites are actually arachnids, like spiders, not mites. They are extremely small – about a half a millimeter – and generally gather on the undersides of leaves. Here they pierce the leaves and suck out the contents to feed. The resulting damage from these feeding spots are very small, pale dots on the tops of foliage that can’t be wiped away, and these speckled leaves are a tell-tale sign of an infestation. As the population of spider mites grows, you’ll start to see fine silk webbing, which can easily be mistaken for dusty houseplant leaves.

    Recent findings suggest that houseplants with broad, thin leaves that are easy to pierce are the most favored. While prayer plants are the most commonly attacked, monstera, alocasia, ficus, croton, palms, English ivy and dracaena are also highly susceptible to these pests.

    According to recent reports, early intervention is the key to success if you have a houseplant with a spider mite infestation. But, even if you're dealing with a heavy infestation, these steps will work, though you'll need to repeat them to break the spider mite lifecycle.

    Industry observers note that it's vital to keep the affected plant away from other houseplants as spider mites can easily move from one plant to another. Move it to a different, plant-free room until the problem has been resolved. Now that you know what to look for, check all your other houseplants very carefully for early, subtle signs of an infestation.

    It has been revealed that next, you want to get rid of as many of the mites as you can. The easiest way to do this is to place your houseplant in the shower or bathtub and give it a good rinse. Use a firm stream of water so the pressure rinses most of the pests off, but ensure the jet isn't so harsh that it damages the plant.

    In a recent development, be sure to direct the water to the undersides of leaves where the mites are feeding and at any webbing you can see. Follow the rinse with a thorough wiping with a damp cloth to remove any webbing still attached. This process is unlikely to remove all the mites or their eggs, so repeat the process every few days as fresh eggs hatch.

    According to recent reports, regular rinsing reduces a spider mite population but it doesn't remove it entirely. To fully break the lifecycle, you'll need an insecticidal soap with a natural formula such as NatureStop Insecticidal Soap, available from Amazon, or a neem oil spray like Captain Jack's Need Oil Spray for Plants, also on Amazon. These organic options will treat indoor plant pests safely. Insecticidal soap kills mites on contact by breaking down their cell membranes, while neem oil disrupts feeding and reproduction and smothers pests.

    Industry observers note that follow the label instructions for whichever product you choose and be sure to cover all areas of the plant, including undersides of leaves and stems. This is important as both products work by direct contact with the mites. Repeat the application as often as suggested on the label, as you’ll likely need several applications to get rid of pests completely.

    Remove any badly damaged leaves, whether they're heavily stippled, have turned mostly yellow or have brown, crispy areas. Snip off with sharp pruners and dispose of them in the garbage (not the compost). Any foliage that's mostly green can be left and, while damaged leaves won’t return to their former glory, healthy areas will still photosynthesize and support the plant’s recovery.

    Good houseplant care in fall will make conditions less favorable to spider mites:.

    Industry observers note that if houseplant leaves have irregular patches of white or light gray powder on their surfaces that can be wiped away, this is likely a fungal infection, powdery mildew and should be treated by disposing of heavily affected leaves and using a product like neem oil or a commercial houseplant fungicide. A white film or larger spots could be mineral deposits from watering If you have hard water and mist or irrigate houseplants from above, easily fixed by cleaning leaves then avoiding getting foliage wet.

    A lost leaf or two doesn’t spell disaster for a Christmas cactus in fall but you can't afford to ignore this distress signal.

But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are.     The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

    Sources indicate that dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

    Dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

    Industry observers note that that doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass. Cool-season grasses perk up a little after the heat of midsummer, but now they’re getting ready for winter dormancy. Some of the tasks you might feel compelled to do now are unnecessary or even harmful.

    Sources indicate that fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder. More fertilizer, more water, and more cutting can do more harm than good this time of year. There is a persistent myth that more care is better, but the truth is that many homeowners do too much.

    According to recent reports, this year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter. Here is a list of typical chores you can skip this year and what to do instead. I promise, this will make your life a lot easier, and your lawn will thank you.

    In a recent development, many homeowners love the look of a pristinely green fall lawn. Others think keeping it totally clear of fall leaves is critical to the turf's health. Keeping the lawn totally clear can be backbreaking work, and it’s not worth the effort.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s true that a dense layer of leaves, especially wet leaves, can harm the grass by trapping moisture and blocking sunlight. But some leaves left in place won’t smother the grass. Also, it’s unnecessary to physically remove every leaf.

    Sources indicate that fall lawns typically need less supplemental water than summer lawns, so ditch your routine watering chore and play it by ear instead. Cooler fall temperatures reduce evaporation, so unless you have unusually dry conditions, you shouldn’t have to water lawns as often as in summer.

    At some point, there will be a final mow of the season, but plan to keep cutting regularly until the grass stops actively growing. Until then, don’t cut grass too short. Your turf needs substantial foliage to collect energy from the sun and build strong, deep roots. Cutting grass short leads to shorter roots, which struggle more through the winter than long roots.

    According to recent reports, as growth slows, you’ll need to cut less frequently. When it’s time to make the final cut, use the lower end of the recommended height range for the grass. It should be at a medium height for winter.

    Instead of bagging cut grass, use a mulching mower. You might want to pick up some of the grass if you have a lot of heavy clumps sitting on the lawn, but most can be kept in place to decompose. The more frequently you mow, the fewer big clumps you'll get.

    Managing weeds in the turf can be a useful fall chore, giving your grass a better chance of getting nutrients and water as it prepares for winter dormancy. However, it’s possible to overwork this chore. Many annual weeds will die as temperatures drop, so don’t bother with these.

    According to recent reports, instead, focus your energy on managing tough perennial weeds. Examples include dandelions, plantain, and clover. Fall is a good time to tackle these with a selective post-emergent herbicide, such as Ortho WeedClear Lawn Weed Killer, provided the weeds are still actively growing and the product is suitable for your grass type. Alternatively, pull them by hand with a tool like Grampa's Weeder, which removes deep-rooted weeds without the need to bend down.

    Sources indicate that fall fertilizing can benefit a lawn, but applying fertilizer automatically or getting the product or timing wrong can waste time and money, or even harm your grass. Warm-season grass is going dormant now, so feeding it can trigger growth that only gets damaged in cooler weather.

    Cool-season grass is different. It’s gathering and storing nutrients in fall and also recovering from summer stress. Fertilizing now can be beneficial if the grass is still growing and the ground hasn't frozen, but be sure to use the right product. You can find fall-specific feeds at garden centers, often called winterizer fertilizers. One popular option is Scotts Turf Builder WinterGuard Fall Lawn Food, which helps lawns recover from summer stress and develop stronger roots ahead of winter.

    Recent findings suggest that your lawn doesn’t have to look perfectly green and manicured in fall to be healthy. Trying to remove every stick, branch, and leaf from the turf is wasted energy. It’s a thankless chore that won’t improve turf health. In fact, leaving some natural material in place benefits the local ecosystem. Next year’s pollinators could be hiding in the leaf litter or the hollowed stem of a fallen branch.

    Instead of aiming for perfection, target your efforts at thinning thick mats of leaves, clearing walkways and drainage areas, and creating designated natural areas. Leave some corners of the garden undisturbed, where wildlife can shelter and survive the winter. Aim for a healthy lawn, not a sterile landscape.

    As you initiative fall lawn chores, remember that type of grass matters. Know what kind of grass you have and what it needs in terms of fall fertilizer, weed protection, and mowing. All homeowners want to give their grass its best chance to come out healthy and green in the spring, but be smart about fall chores. Be selective about your efforts this time of year and focus on those tasks that will actually make a difference to the health of your lawn.
