    For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

    Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

    With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

    The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

    Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

    Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:.

    âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â.

    Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person. The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

    It has been revealed that beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

    Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

    Industry observers note that this is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

    Sources indicate that emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

    Sources indicate that they are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

    Recent findings suggest that ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

    Sources indicate that while there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

    This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:.

    Is this dog required because of a disability?

    What task has it been trained to perform?

    It has been revealed that thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

    News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

    Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

    If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

    According to recent reports, cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is vital to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

    Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

    If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

    Talk to your vet about a payment plan, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

    Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most important first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

But there's a difference between a pup who has always slept with their legs in the air and one who suddenly starts acting strangely. But a predisposition doesn't guarantee a particular behavior, nor does it explain every individual habit. A dog's behavior comes from a combination of biology and learned experience, which is often less convenient than blaming everything on their breed, but it is much closer to reality.

    Industry observers note that A 2022 study published in Science looked at the behavior and DNA of thousands of dogs. In other words, dogs of the same breed can have very different personalities and behaviors. Genetics plays a role, but it doesn't tell the whole story.

    That doesn't mean genetics is irrelevant. The researchers found evidence that many behavioral traits do have a heritable component. Rather, the findings show why breed alone is a poor crystal ball for predicting how an individual dog will behave.

    #90732. November Is the Perfect Time to Plant These 6 Fruit Trees – You'll Enjoy Delicious Harvests for Years

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1756 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    November Is the Perfect Time to Plant These 6 Fruit Trees – You'll Enjoy Delicious Harvests for Years

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In France, gardeners and farmers have a saying that November 25 – the day Saint Catherine is celebrated – is the ideal day to plant a tree.
    • Growing fruit trees is a gift to yourself that keeps on giving.
    • Which fruit trees should top your list?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In France, gardeners and farmers have a saying that November 25 – the day Saint Catherine is celebrated – is the ideal day to plant a tree. ("À la Sainte-Catherine, tout bois prend racine.”) That may not apply literally to every tree species, but I can tell you this much: November is an excellent time to plant many kinds of fruit trees as long as the ground is not frozen.

    Growing fruit trees is a gift to yourself that keeps on giving. Each tree in your home orchard can provide delicious homegrown harvests for years to come. Planting fruit trees in November offers many benefits. The cooler late-fall weather reduces transplanting stress, and seasonal rains keep the soil moist. That helps the trees establish roots before spring growth begins.

    Which fruit trees should top your list? Many wonderful fruit trees are great to plant in November, so choose the one that grows your favorite fruit. But be sure to consider your local climate. Each fruit tree species has its own hardiness zone that indicates its cold tolerance. Some – like apples and pears – also have winter chilling requirements. You’ll also want to consider the mature size of the tree and be certain it will fit into your landscape.

    Does life get any better than wandering out to the backyard and pulling a crisp apple right off your own tree and taking a bite? So when you consider planting a tree in November, don’t overlook apples. Apple trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–8, depending on the variety. You can plant either a bare-root apple tree or a container-grown tree in November, as long as the soil is not frozen, although spring planting is often safer in colder zones 3–4.

    There are many apple varieties to choose from. Most won’t fruit reliably on their own, so check their pollination requirements when you purchase your tree. Your tree may require a compatible cross-pollinator that flowers at the same time. For a great pairing, try a ‘Honeycrisp’ apple tree alongside a ‘Gala’ apple tree – both available from Trees.com – which can cross-pollinate and give you two delicious varieties to harvest. If you only have room for one tree, ‘Golden Delicious’ is partially self-fertile and can produce fruit without a partner, although you'll generally get a better crop with cross-pollination.

    Plant your apple tree in a full sun location in well-draining soil. You may want to stake the tree to prevent any windrock until its roots anchor it well. You can buy a tree-staking kit from Amazon, but if your area is very windy, a crossbar attached to two posts will provide more support.

    Pears feel like a fancier fruit than apples, but the trees are just as easy to grow and maintain. Like pear slices in your salad? With your own pear tree, you can pick sweet fruit anytime during the harvest season. Pear trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–10, depending on the variety.

    Like apple trees, pear trees grow best in a full sun location in well-draining soil. As with most apple trees, pear trees are not usually self-pollinating. That means that you will need two compatible cultivars for reliable pollination and fruit set. However, there are exceptions. Both the ‘Bartlett’ pear tree and ‘Kieffer’ pear tree, available from Garden Goods Direct, are partially self-fertile, although they generally produce better crops with a suitable pollination partner. Kieffer also offers good resistance to fire blight, making it worth considering in areas where this disease is a concern.

    Recent findings suggest that november can be a good time to plant a bare-root pear tree in milder regions. The plant is dormant, but its root system can continue to grow during the winter as long as the soil remains sufficiently warm and unfrozen. It is also possible to plant container trees in November. Be sure the planting hole is several times as wide as the root system, but no deeper than the root ball.

    Industry observers note that if you want a tree with sweet, juicy fruit, consider planting a plum tree. The fruit is delicious when eaten fresh, but also makes great compotes or jams. Plum trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 4–9, depending on the variety. November is a good month to plant bare-root plum trees in milder regions, and it’s suitable for container-grown plum trees as well. Just don’t wait too long since you can't plant after the ground is frozen. In colder zones, spring planting is often safer.

    Industry observers note that most fruit trees need sunny locations, and plum trees are not an exception. In fact, it’s particularly important to select a good site since plums flower very early in spring. If your tree is in a low-lying frost pocket, the blossoms will be vulnerable to late frosts. You should also pick a site that offers protection from harsh winds. Plant your plum in cool, well-draining soil. Wet, heavy soil can lead to root disease.

    Industry observers note that most plum trees require a pollinator, so you’ll need to plant two compatible trees. However, several varieties are self-fertile, so a single tree is enough to produce a harvest. One great option is the ‘Methley’ plum tree, available from Trees.com, which produces sweet, juicy fruit without needing a pollination partner.

    Sources indicate that most of us know that a peach tree is a deciduous tree with juicy round fruits. Here’s a lesser-known fact: the same botanical species can grow fuzzy fruits, called peaches, or glossy-skinned fruits, called nectarines. Peach trees generally thrive in USDA hardiness zones 5–8, although this varies by variety. Peach trees, especially bare-root peach trees, can be successfully planted in November, as long as the ground is not frozen. In colder regions, however, spring planting is often safer.

    Sources indicate that peach trees need sunny sites. Plant yours where it will get at least 6–8 hours a day of direct sun. This is essential to trigger flower buds and sweeten the fruit. The soil should be well-draining since standing water will rot the tree’s roots. If the tree is grafted, be sure to set the tree in the planting hole so that the graft union sits above the soil line.

    Sources indicate that peach trees also need a specific amount of winter cold, chill hours, when temperatures fall within the range of approximately 32°F to 45°F (0°C to 7°C). Standard peach varieties need from 650 to 1,050 chill hours, although you can find low-chill types that need as few as 100 hours.

    Recent findings suggest that one great option for colder regions is the ‘Red Haven’ peach tree from Trees.com, a self-fertile variety that produces sweet, juicy peaches and needs around 800–900 chill hours. For warmer regions with mild winters, try ‘Tropic Snow,’ a low-chill variety that needs just 225 chill hours and produces deliciously sweet, white-fleshed peaches.

    The American persimmon is among our most overlooked native fruit trees. This species does not get the spotlight given to apple, peach, or pear trees, yet it offers so much: edible fruit, wildlife habitat, and attractive fall foliage. The fruit is an crucial food source for wild birds and mammals, including raccoons, opossums, and foxes, and it remains available into early winter, when many other food sources have diminished.

    Native to the eastern and southeastern United States, these trees are very cold-hardy, thriving in USDA hardiness zones 4–9. You can buy a common American persimmon tree from Plant Addicts to enjoy its fruit and seasonal interest in your own backyard. American persimmons typically have separate male and female trees, but some varieties are self-fertile and can produce fruit without a pollination partner. If you're growing a tree for its fruit, check its pollination requirements before buying.

    The trees can grow to between 35 and 60 feet (10–18 m) tall, although they can be kept smaller by pruning. The fruit they produce is orange and initially astringent, but it becomes sweet and delicious when it fully ripens, often around the time of the first frost.

    November is a good time to plant an American persimmon tree in milder regions. You cannot plant at this time, however, if the ground is frozen. Find a well-drained area with loamy, organically rich soil in a full sun location. Avoid frost pockets since these trees may be damaged by unseasonable frosts.

    Fig trees have a long and somewhat exotic history. They have been cultivated for 12,000 years and are among the earliest domesticated plants. They have deep symbolic meaning as symbols of peace and prosperity, but, perhaps more vital to modern gardeners, the trees are tough, drought-tolerant, and resistant to pests and diseases.

    Recent findings suggest that fig trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 6–11, depending on the variety, although those in colder zones may need winter protection. For a reliable, sweet-fruited variety, try the ‘Brown Turkey’ fig from Nature Hills, which is well suited to milder regions. Gardeners in colder zones might prefer the ‘Chicago Hardy’ fig, also available from Nature Hills, which can withstand much lower winter temperatures with suitable protection. Both varieties are self-fruitful, so you only need one tree to enjoy a harvest.

    Industry observers note that if you live in USDA zone 8 or above, it is generally appropriate to plant your tree in November, provided the ground isn't frozen. In cooler zones, you should wait until spring. For November planting, select a full-sun location, ideally against a south- or southwest-facing wall. This helps the tree capture and retain warmth. The soil must be well-draining and slightly acidic. Water the tree deeply right after planting to settle the soil around the roots.

    Once the tree is planted, apply a layer of organic mulch around the base, keeping the mulch a few inches away from the actual trunk to prevent rot.

    In a recent development, teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

    • Industry observers note that “Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” mentioned U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.

    “This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” remarked Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Cybercriminals who terrorize American businesses cannot evade justice by operating from abroad or hiding behind sophisticated technology. Artem Stryzhak’s sentence underscores the Justice Department’s resolve to dismantle ransomware groups, hold them accountable, and protect American businesses and people from cyber extortion.”.

    Industry observers note that “Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of Latest York. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”.

    “Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We are proud of our law enforcement partners for their skilled investigative work in bringing this criminal to justice.”.

    “Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” remarked Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Branch. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners. Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”.

    According to court documents, Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, Spain, conspired with others to perpetrate ransomware attacks on behalf of multiple ransomware groups against victim computer networks in the United States and other countries. The conspiracies caused significant damage to victim computer systems. Beginning in approximately June 2021, Stryzhak joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate. Stryzhak was given access to the Nefilim ransomware and agreed with one of the Nefilim ransomware group administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the Nefilim administrators, including Tymoshchuk, 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims in exchange for Stryzhak’s access to the Nefilim ransomware.

    The ransomware attacks that Stryzhak conducted with Nefilim ransomware included a June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole data from a company in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, Stryzhak created email addresses that were incorporated in a ransom note sent to the victim company. Stryzhak conspired with the Nefilim ransomware actors until at least October 2021. If a victim paid the ransom demand, the perpetrators provided the decryption key, enabling the victim to decrypt files locked by the ransomware.

    Sources indicate that also according to court documents, Stryzhak separately joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive conspirators attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals, and businesses. Hive ransomware attacks caused major disruptions in victim daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. In one case, a hospital attacked by the Hive ransomware group had to forgo digital technology to treat existing patients and was unable to accept upcoming patients immediately following the attack.

    In his role as a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators deployed Hive ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dentist office, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. Victims were unable to access their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long disruption campaign against the Hive ransomware group, provided a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, thereby allowing that victim to decrypt its encrypted data without having to pay a ransom.

    Stryzhak was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. Stryzhak pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

    Recent findings suggest that the FBI Springfield Field Office investigated the Nefilim ransomware case and the FBI Tampa Field Office investigated the Hive ransomware case. The Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs, the FBI’s Newly introduced York Field Office, and Spanish law enforcement authorities provided substantial assistance locating, arresting, and extraditing Stryzhak.

    Acting Assistant Deputy Chief James S. Yoon of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), former CCIPS Senior Trial Attorney Brian Z. Mund, and Assistant United States Attorneys Alexander F. Mindlin and Ellen H. Sise of the Eastern District of New York’s National Security and Cybercrime Section prosecuted the Nefilim ransomware case. CCIPS Trial Attorneys Alison M. Zitron and Christen M. Gallagher and Assistant United States Attorney Hannah Watson of the Middle District of Florida prosecuted the Hive ransomware case.

    Industry observers note that the U.S. Department of State’s Transnational Organized Crime (TOC) Rewards Program has offered a reward of up to $11 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction or location of Stryzhak’s charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. Anyone with information about Tymoshchuk should contact the FBI via phone at +1-917-242-1407, by email at TymoTips@fbi.gov, by contacting your local field office, if in the United States, or by contacting the nearest U.S. Embassy, if located overseas. More information about the Tymoshchuk TOC reward offer and one related to Hive ransomware is located on the State Department website.

    CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 180 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $350 million in victim funds.

    While nighttime zoomies are a well-recognized phenomenon in the feline world, it turns out dogs can also get a little over-excited at the prospect of bedtime. Just as the house is settling down for the night, a dog may start bouncing around, digging into the blankets, or demanding attention.

    It also turns out that there isn't a single explanation for this evening burst of energy; there are several. The bed itself can be exciting, particularly because it smells like a favorite person and offers a chance for interaction. In other cases, a dog may simply have energy left to burn. Understanding the possible reasons can help explain why bedtime sometimes turns into playtime.

    Dogs spend much of their time looking up at people from the floor. Climbing onto a bed changes that perspective, bringing a dog much closer to its owner's face and making interaction easier.

    That alone can be enough to spark a playful mood. A dog may drop into a play bow, bark for attention, or bounce around in an attempt to encourage its person to join in.

    Being face to face can make play feel more inviting, particularly for dogs that enjoy close interaction with their owners. What looks like a sudden burst of energy may simply be a dog making the most of the opportunity to engage on a different level.

    A bed carries the scent of the person who sleeps in it, making it an especially interesting place for a dog to explore. Dogs rely heavily on their noses to understand their surroundings, and familiar smells can be particularly appealing.

    For a dog that enjoys spending time with its owner, the bed may be one of the most comforting and interesting places in the home. Rolling around on the sheets or sniffing the blankets lets a dog investigate those familiar scents while enjoying a spot associated with its favorite person.

    That combination of comfort, familiarity, and excitement can help explain why some dogs become especially playful once they climb onto the mattress.

    In a recent development, for dogs that love burrowing, a bed covered in sheets and blankets can feel like an invitation to play. Digging, wriggling underneath the covers, and pushing through folds of fabric can all become part of the fun.

    Recent findings suggest that some breeds are particularly inclined toward this kind of behavior. Dachshunds, for example, were bred to pursue animals such as badgers and weasels into their burrows. Their instinct to dig and tunnel can make a pile of blankets especially appealing. Meanwhile, Chihuahuas seem to be particularly fond of burrowing into the warmth and security of their humanâs bed.

    A dog that discovers the pleasure of diving between the sheets may promptly turn it into a regular bedtime activity.

    Recent findings suggest that dogs are often quick to learn which behaviors get a reaction from their owners. Climbing onto the bed puts them right where they're difficult to ignore, particularly if they start bouncing around or nudging someone for attention.

    It has been revealed that bedtime can also signal that the day is winding down and an opportunity for cuddling is approaching. A dog that enjoys being close to its owner may become excited at the prospect of spending that time together.

    If playful behavior consistently earns attention, a dog may be encouraged to repeat it. What begins as a burst of excitement can become a familiar part of the nightly routine. Even if this nightly ritual isnât one you welcome, waving arms and raised voices often count as a positive interaction for a dog, so if youâre trying to get your dog off the bed, be careful your methods align with your message.

    Sometimes, a dog becomes especially energetic at bedtime simply because theyâre not ready to settle down. If it hasn't had enough exercise or stimulation during the day, the bed may become an outlet for that leftover energy.

    A dog that is still eager to run, jump, and play may need more activity before the household turns in for the night. An evening walk or a game of tug-of-war can help provide an opportunity to burn off some energy before bedtime.

    A dog that's had enough exercise and stimulation is more likely to be ready to relax, rather than treating the mattress as a playground.

    Many owners enjoy sleeping alongside their dogs, while others prefer to keep their beds pet-free. Sharing a bed can feel cozy and comforting, and having a dog nearby may also be soothing for people who experience anxiety or other mental health challenges.

    Recent findings suggest that there are practical considerations, too. Dogs can carry dirt, bacteria, and parasites into the bed, and some owners would rather not have fur on their sheets or pillows.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, whether a dog is allowed to sleep on the bed comes down to what works for the household. If itâs not a problem, then itâs not a problem. There's no single right choice, and a dog can still enjoy plenty of affection and companionship without sharing the mattress.

    If you do want your bed to be a dog-free zone, the simplest solution is to keep the bedroom door closed. But if youâre simply looking for a way to get them off the bed without it turning into a party, a calm and quiet approach is best. A single command or using a slip-lead to silently guide them off the bed will be far more effective than shouting and pointing.

    A dog getting frisky on the bed is often responding to a combination of familiar scents, opportunities for attention, and the chance to play somewhere comfortable. Blankets can add to the appeal, especially for dogs that enjoy burrowing.

    Recent findings suggest that if the behavior seems excessive, however, it may be worth looking at how much exercise and stimulation the dog gets during the day. Adding a walk or play session before bed can help make the transition to sleep easier.

    According to recent reports, for many dogs, the bed is simply an exciting place to be close to their favorite person. With a little preparation, bedtime can still end in a peaceful night's sleep rather than an impromptu wrestling match.

    The most rewarding part of working in emergency veterinary medicine? When the patient is feeling good enough to try to bite you!

    #90727. National Security Division Reveals First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

    National Security Division Reveals First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

    📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
    • The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.
    • This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

    The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

    This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution. While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

    It has been revealed that “This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” noted Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”.

    According to recent reports, “HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” mentioned Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”.

    The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

    In a recent development, pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

    According to recent reports, between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

    Industry observers note that although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

    The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

    According to recent reports, this case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

    Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

    Industry observers note that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    Industry observers note that nearly 30 dogs have arrived in Newly introduced York after being rescued from a dog-meat farm in South Korea. Their journey toward adoption is beginning, but with the country's ban still months away from taking full effect, the work is far from over.

    A plane ride to Latest York probably wasn't on these dogs' bingo cards. Neither, for that matter, was a soft bed, a full bowl of food, or the chance to be someone's beloved family member. After spending their lives confined to cages, even the simplest things may seem exciting and new.

    Sources indicate that on October 1, nearly 30 dogs were rescued from a dog-meat farm in Gangjin, South Korea, that once bred and slaughtered as many as 1,000 dogs each year. This was part of a larger rescue operation by Humane World for Animals that saved more than 70 dogs from the property.

    For the organization, the operation marks its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea ahead of the country's ban, which takes full effect on February 7, 2027. Humane World for Animals has rescued nearly 3,000 dogs from farms since 2015, making this a significant milestone.

    In a recent development, and yes, it's a reason to celebrate. But before we get too comfortable patting ourselves on the back, there's a much bigger picture to consider. Getting these dogs out was a huge victory, but there are still thousands at risk.

    When the rescue team arrived at the farm in Gangjin, in South Korea's South Jeolla Province, they were met with disturbing scenes. Rows of rusting cages, abandoned collars scattered on the ground, and skeletal remains served as a gruesome reminder of the dogs that hadn't been so lucky.

    Industry observers note that it's a hard reality to come to terms with, especially if your own dog is at the moment hogging the sofa, demanding snacks, or staring at you as though you've ruined their life by being five minutes late with dinner. The minor dramas faced by our beloved pets are a world away from what these poor dogs endured.

    Humane World for Animals has reported finding mixed breeds and dogs of different sizes during its rescue work. The survivors included Jindos, a breed native to South Korea, a husky mix, and smaller dogs, including a spitz mix. In other words, any dog could end up on the menu.

    In this most recent rescue, a concerned citizen alerted a local animal protection group, which contacted Humane World for Animals and the authorities. Officials found that the farm had broken South Korea's Animal Protection Act. The farmer, a man in his 80s, agreed to hand over the dogs and promised not to take part in the dog-meat trade again.

    Industry observers note that more than 70 dogs were rescued. Nearly 30 travelled to Fresh York, another 12 went to a rehabilitation center in Montreal, and some mothers and their puppies remained in South Korea because they were too young to fly safely.

    According to recent reports, rescuing dogs from situations like this isn't as simple as just opening a cage and booking the next available flight. International transport requires veterinary checks, vaccinations, documentation, and careful consideration about which animals are fit to travel. The priority is getting them out safely, not rushing them onto a plane for the sake of a happy headline.

    South Korea passed its Special Act on the Termination of Breeding, Slaughter, and Distribution of Dogs for Consumption in January 2024. Its key prohibitions will finally take full effect on February 7, 2027, making it illegal to breed, slaughter, or sell dogs or dog meat for human consumption. But the transition is already underway.

    Sources indicate that in May 2026, South Korea's Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs reported that about 82% of the country's 1,537 registered dog-meat farms had closed. Over a thousand farms closed is something worth celebrating, but it means 272 farms are still operating.

    Another consideration is that closing a farm doesn't automatically save the dogs living there. A business can shut down, the gates can close, and the paperwork can be signed, but where do all those dogs go?

    According to recent reports, according to Humane World for Animals, government figures indicate that of approximately 393,857 dogs counted on farms that had been closed, only 1,121 were adopted or transferred to public shelters. That's about 0.3%.

    Itâs understood that most of these dogs were sent for slaughter or moved to other farms. So, while the closure of dog meat farms is good news, itâs not a true victory if these dogs are simply moved on to face the same fate. The ban is a huge step forward, but a law is only as good as its enforcement.

    Sources indicate that the real goal isn't just to close the farms. It's making sure the dogs are actually safe.

    It has been revealed that getting out of the farm is the first big hurdle for these dogs. Now comes veterinary care, recovery, and the not-so-small task of learning how to live in a completely different world.

    In a recent development, humane World for Animalsâ rescue protocols include veterinary exams, vaccinations, respiratory screening when needed, and the health documents required for international travel. Each dog has their own needs. Some may need treatment for skin problems, wounds, dental disease, or nutritional deficiencies.

    It has been revealed that the second, and perhaps most challenging, hurdle for these dogs is adapting to a whole fresh way of life. Just because a dog has been saved doesn't automatically mean a dog feels safe.

    Imagine never having lived in a home, then suddenly finding yourself surrounded by doors, stairs, strange noises, slippery floors, and humans who keep trying to show you how much they love you. Even a well-meaning hug could be overwhelming. And the vacuum cleaner? Let's just say it probably won't be winning any popularity contests.

    Recent findings suggest that these dogs may need to learn things many pets take for granted: how to explore a room, relax around people, or understand that a hand reaching toward them isn't something to fear. Some will be curious from the start. Others may prefer to watch from a safe distance. Neither response is wrong, and patience plus a little common sense go a long way.

    In a recent development, A quiet place to rest, a predictable routine, and the freedom to explore without being pushed can help a dog settle in. Rewarding small steps with positive reinforcement builds confidence without turning every upcoming experience into a test.

    Adjusting to a new life takes time, and there's no need to rush it. A dog who hides under the table on day one isn't a failed adoption. A dog who isn't ready for cuddles isn't being ungrateful. Theyâre figuring things out, and they need time to decide that this strange new place might actually be safe. Building trust and confidence can be a slow process.

    Those familiar with the process of adopting or fostering dogs, particularly those who may not have had the best start to life, may have heard of the 3-3-3 Rule for Dogs: 3 days, 3 weeks, 3 months. Itâs a simplified interpretation of the timeline many dogs tend to follow when adjusting to a upcoming home environment.

    The first 3 days are about decompression and resetting the nervous system. It might look like a dog that is timid, constantly moving, hiding, or even showing signs of aggression. Some dogs adjust swiftly, while others may take a little longer than 3 days. The vital thing to know is that this version of the dog is not usually a good representation of their true selves.

    Over the first 3 weeks, dogs will start to gain confidence and explore their newly introduced world. They are often testing boundaries, becoming familiar with patterns, and learning how to trust. Being consistent and providing predictable routines is paramount to this process.

    It has been revealed that by the time 3 months have passed, most dogs will be feeling more settled. It may still take some time for their full personality to appear, but with every passing month, they become more confident, more trusting, and less anxious.

    Sometimes progress looks like taking a treat from someone's hand. Sometimes it's finally falling asleep without startling at every sound. Those moments might not make a flashy before-and-after video, but for that dog, they're a major deal.

    One more thing: fear and behavioural changes shouldn't automatically be dismissed as consequences of a dog's past. Pain, illness, and other medical problems can affect behaviour, too. If a dog seems persistently distressed or suddenly starts acting differently, a veterinary check is important. We don't want to assume it's trauma when there may be pain due to a treatable medical issue behind it.

    According to recent reports, A second chance isn't just getting a dog out of a cage. It's giving them the medical care, space, and time to discover that life can be safe, and maybe even pretty wonderful.

    Humane World for Animals calls the Gangjin operation its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea. But that doesn't mean the work is over. The organization plans to continue monitoring the ban and supporting efforts to enforce it.

    Industry observers note that closing farms is a huge win. Full stop. But making sure dogs aren't left behind, moved elsewhere, or subjected to illegal practices is part of making that win count. With the ban taking full effect in February 2027, the coming months will be crucial.

    For the dogs already rescued, a upcoming life is finally within reach. Veterinary care. Rehabilitation. A chance to find a home where the biggest worry is whether they get the good spot on the sofa. That's quite the upgrade.

    According to recent reports, now, we turn our attention to the dogs still waiting in South Koreaâs remaining farms. Stopping the dog meat trade is a huge victory, but in many ways, itâs just the beginning. Saving these dogs is more than just stopping the slaughter. Itâs making sure they all get the happy ending they deserve.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    In a recent development, dogs have been a fixture of family life for thousands of years, and many people who grew up with one say they canât picture their childhood without them. Beyond the obvious benefits of companionship and fun, growing up with a dog has been shown to have positive effects on physical and emotional well-being; advantages that show up in how children handle friendships, feelings, and everyday challenges.

    It has been revealed that of course, this doesnât mean that having a dog is right for everyone. Bringing a dog into your home is a major decision that affects budgets and daily routines for years to come, and the best outcomes tend to come from families who go in with open eyes.

    For anyone considering life with a dog, here are a few ways they can improve a childâs life, and things to consider before adopting one.

    Growing up around animals can lower the chance of developing allergies later on. Dogs, and all the things that come with living with them, expose children to a range of allergens, which helps build a more robust immune system. The key seems to be early exposure, which means the sooner a dog becomes part of a childâs world, the better.

    According to recent reports, children who are close to their dogs tend to be more securely attached to their parents, and theyâre more likely to form strong friendships, too. Strong relationships in one part of a childâs life seem to go hand in hand with strong relationships in others. Kids who share more physical contact with their dogs, from cuddles to roughhousing, tend to get along better with their moms, dads, and friends.

    Recent findings suggest that kids who grow up with a family dog tend to have lower rates of anxiety. The benefits reach well beyond childhood, too. Dogs can ease feelings of depression and anxiety in adults who went through childhood trauma, and they can reduce signs of post-traumatic stress, which is part of the reason theyâre so often brought into therapy.

    In a recent development, A dog is a living, breathing creature with needs, and children who help care for one learn responsibility and dependability. A five-year-old canât take on every chore, but age-appropriate tasks are a great place to start. Young children spend much of their lives at the mercy of parents and teachers, so having a dog to look after can give them a real sense of empowerment and build self-esteem.

    Caring for an animal from an early age also builds empathy, which supports emotional intelligence and helps a child grow into a more compassionate person. The lessons go on from there. Dogs model loyalty; training and bonding teach patience, and learning to read a dogâs body language and respect their boundaries teaches respect. When a family pet eventually passes away, children also learn about death and grieving.

    It has been revealed that children with pets tend to have better self-esteem than children without them. The effect appears to be strongest as kids approach adolescence; an age when the emotional support of a companion animal may matter most.

    Families with dogs tend to be more physically active than their peers, getting about 11 extra minutes of exercise a day. That may not sound like much, but it adds up to roughly 5.5 hours a month in a society that is growing more sedentary all the time.

    Industry observers note that for some children, the effect is far larger. Girls in particular gained around 52 minutes of light physical activity a day after a dog joined the family. The flip side was striking too, since girls who lost their pet saw their daily activity drop by 62 minutes.

    In a recent development, children tend to handle stressful moments better with a dog nearby. They feel happier and more at ease, and being able to touch the dog calms them even further. Simply having a furry companion close by seems to help kids feel steadier inside.

    For all the upsides, adopting a dog isnât a decision to take lightly, and there are a few things every family needs to consider before racing out to get a four-legged friend.

    Budget: Dogs depend on their owners for food, veterinary care, and emergencies, and a household budget that canât cover those costs is a reason to rethink the blueprint.

    Age: Although many childhood benefits increase the earlier they start living with a dog, sometimes waiting until children are older is a good idea. St. Bernards make fantastic family pets, for example, but they can weigh as much as 180 pounds and can hurt a child accidentally. Small breeds have their own risks, since they can be fragile and prone to injury until kids learn boundaries and how to respect animals.

    Industry observers note that lifestyle: A family that works long hours and spends every evening shuttling children to activities needs a plan for what the dog will be doing. Not every schedule has room for a pet, and that is perfectly fine, but a dog shouldnât be adopted without free time to spend with it.

    Motivation: Children often beg for a dog, promising to walk, feed, and pick up after them.

    Then, the novelty fades, and the adults end up with the bulk of the care. Although itâs a good idea to encourage children to take on some of the responsibility of looking after a dog, you should assume that youâll be the one doing most of the work â hope for the best, plan for the worst!

    Growing up alongside a dog can bring real benefits, from fewer allergies and lower anxiety to stronger relationships and more time spent moving. But to enjoy the benefits of living with a dog, families need to have the time, money, and genuine desire to take care of one.

    Growing up with a dog might not guarantee health and happiness, but itâs a pretty good place to start!

    Industry observers note that robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse are fast becoming the it couple of the moment (not least of all because the man formerly known as Edward Cullen is now Bond, James Bond). So you'd best believe they're setting trends left, right, and center – even in the world of indoor gardening.

    In a recent development, and while we'd expect the pair to have a suitably impressive garden, it turns out their houseplant of choice is considerably more interesting than your average monstera or spider plant. In fact, it's a miniature tree with a rather sophisticated reputation: the not-so-humble bonsai!

    Sources indicate that yes, with the couple's busy schedules taking them between different homes and locations, it makes sense that they're all about the idea of bringing greenery indoors. After all, houseplants offer a lovely way to make a space feel personal, even when you're not necessarily putting down roots for the long term. And if you're going to invest in an indoor plant, then why not make it something a little more unusual?

    Speaking to the Perfectly Imperfect Newsletter in September 2024, Suki Waterhouse revealed that she developed a rather unexpected obsession with bonsai trees during the final month of her pregnancy.

    In a recent development, 'When I was preggers in the last month and didn’t really feel like seeing anyone, I got obsessed with getting a bonsai tree,' she says. 'I found a number on Google and pulled up to a house in East Hollywood and a lady had a bunch of them locked up in her back garden. Felt super cool and mysterious. Some of them she’d had for 30 years. Fell in love with this guy and have become obsessed with pruning.'.

    The leaves on this bonsai fold up at night or in subdued light, and it wakes up when we do!

    It's a wonderfully specific plant obsession, and one we can absolutely get behind. Especially as there's something rather magical about a tiny tree that's been carefully cultivated for decade; there's a reason that bonsai is as much an art form as it is a gardening hobby.

    Of course, Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson aren't the only ones who appreciate the appeal of the beautiful bonsai tree. In fact, there's been something of a growing appreciation for the slower, more mindful side of gardening, and bonsai? Why, that fits the philosophy rather beautifully.

    Sources indicate that more importantly? Well, despite the fact that bonsai trees have a reputation for being (whisper it) high-maintenance, they're not as intimidating as their appearance might suggest. The trick is choosing the right one – so look for a variety suited to indoor conditions and make a note of its basic requirements. And, as Suki herself pointed out, a little regular pruning and thoughtful watering can go a long way.

    If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have inspired you to introduce a little bonsai magic into your own home, there are a few varieties worth considering...

    Recent findings suggest that if you're new to bonsai, ficus is arguably the best place to start. These tropical trees are considerably more forgiving than many traditional bonsai varieties and adapt well to indoor conditions. Their glossy leaves and interesting roots make them particularly striking, too.

    Give something like this Small Ficus Live Bonsai Tree from Brussell's Bonsai a bright position with plenty of indirect light, keep it away from cold draughts and water when the top layer of compost begins to dry.

    If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have got you in the mood for something a little more unusual, consider the Hawaiian umbrella tree (Schefflera arboricola).

    This bonsai's distinctive leaves and naturally branching growth make it a particularly attractive choice for an indoor plant.

    It's also relatively tolerant of indoor humidity levels and can cope with slightly less-than-perfect light conditions, although a bright spot will always help it thrive. Take care to allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings, and prune regularly to maintain its shape.

    A lovely option for anyone who tends to be a little forgetful with watering, jade bonsai (Crassula ovata) is a succulent that enjoys plenty of bright light and needs much less frequent watering than tropical bonsai varieties.

    Pick up something like this Live Jade from Brussell's Bonsai, let the compost dry out thoroughly between waterings, and make sure it's planted in a free-draining bonsai mix to prevent its roots from sitting in excess moisture.

    Industry observers note that of course, even the most beginner-friendly bonsai isn't quite a plant you can forget about. Even Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse will tell you, light, watering and occasional pruning are all key, and it's worth remembering that not every bonsai is suited to indoor living.

    As a general rule of thumb, tropical and subtropical varieties are generally the best choice for growing inside; most traditional temperate trees need to experience the changing seasons outdoors.

    Sources indicate that still, there's something rather lovely about the idea of tending to a little tree that could stay with you for decades. And if Suki Waterhouse's experience is anything to go by, it might just become your next very absorbing, very cool, very mysterious hobby.

    It has been revealed that long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

    It has been revealed that stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in Upcoming Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

    It has been revealed that when the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

    Once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

    Industry observers note that after surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

    According to recent reports, stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

    According to recent reports, during the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

    Stubby returned home a celebrity. He led parades, attended war bond rallies, and met three sitting or future presidents: Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

    Conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

    Stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a newly introduced generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

    Sources indicate that stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

    In a recent development, every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

    It has been revealed that support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

    It has been revealed that learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

    Industry observers note that keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

    Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

    According to recent reports, these dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

    According to recent reports, if Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

    Industry observers note that I have a question about my dog, Jethro. Sometimes when he alerts, the hackles between his shoulders rise. Other times they are prominent along his lower back. What does each appearance indicate about how he is responding?â.

    That is a great observation! When a dogâs hackles rise, it is an involuntary response controlled by the autonomic nervous system called piloerection, and it tells us that his arousal level has increased. However, the location of the raised hair does not reliably tell us which emotion a dog is experiencing.

    Sources indicate that when the hackles rise between his shoulders, it can accompany alertness, excitement, uncertainty, or concern. When they appear along his lower back, the same range of emotional responses is possible. Neither pattern automatically indicates aggression, fear, or a particular level of threat. Think of hackles as a little emotional alarm bell; they tell us Jethro is experiencing heightened arousal, but not exactly why.

    Industry observers note that different dogs will respond to different stimuli in different ways, so thereâs no âone size fits allâ explanation for why different areas are triggered. I would pay close attention to what is happening around him when this occurs. Is he alerting to a stranger approaching the house, another dog walking past, an unfamiliar noise, or something unexpected in the environment? You might want to start keeping a record of what is going on before and after Jethroâs hackles are raised, and whether itâs his shoulders or lower back that is involved.

    In a recent development, combine that context with his facial expression, ear position, tail carriage, posture, muscle tension, and ability to disengage. Looking at the whole picture helps us understand whether Jethro is curious, excited, uncertain, or uncomfortable, and, most importantly, how we can best support him. These details, together with what triggered the alert, give us a much clearer picture of how Jethro is feeling.

    I Save Old Bubble Wrap Every Fall for This Budget Garden Winterizing Trick

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All year, I save up bubble wrap to use as a cheap DIY solution to see my garden through the winter.
    • If you're a fan of container gardening, you'll know that the temperature of soil in planters is so much more erratic than in the ground, leaving roots riding a right rollercoaster of conditions.
    • A DIY pot-wrap also helps to stop plants from drying out.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All year, I save up bubble wrap to use as a cheap DIY solution to see my garden through the winter. My trick is simple: I sandwich bubble wrap between a folded rectangle of burlap and wrap it around patio pots. Those little pockets of air act as excellent insulation, but my burlap and bubble-wrap pot-cozy does so much more than help to keep borderline-tender plants alive through winter.

    If you're a fan of container gardening, you'll know that the temperature of soil in planters is so much more erratic than in the ground, leaving roots riding a right rollercoaster of conditions. By insulating pots, I save my plants a whole heap of stress, which means they can use their precious energy for far more exciting things. Winter-flowering pansies and violas in pots can stall in a cold snap, but stop that soil from freezing solid around their shallow roots and the plants will carry on pushing out their cheery petals. Winter-flowering heather in planters, too, will bloom far more steadily if their root balls are protected.

    A DIY pot-wrap also helps to stop plants from drying out. When soil freezes – and it’ll freeze far sooner and deeper in a planter than in the ground – roots can’t access its moisture. If the plant keeps losing water through its leaves (and remember the wind strips moisture from foliage just as readily as the sun), it’s no different to drought conditions. And when a plant is losing more water than it can replace, it goes into survival mode. For early-flowering shrubs like Daphne odora and ornamental camellias, that can mean dropped buds and zero blooms.

    Wrapping also helps to stop pots from cracking in the continual freeze-thaw of winter, especially if they're made from porous terracotta. And let’s not forget those borderline-hardy plants either: with their roots already safely insulated in bubble wrap and burlap in late fall, it’s a super-quick job to zip up shrubs in frost jackets when a cold spell is forecast.

    It’s best to combine bubble wrap with good-quality, tightly-woven burlap on a roll such as this from Walmart to insulate pots. Cut a rectangle of burlap that’s twice the height of the pot and long enough to wrap all the way around with a generous overlap. Then fold the burlap in two and lay bubble wrap in between the two layers. Tie this around the pot with heavy-duty twine or rope, being careful not to cover the soil surface.

    There are so many other uses for these low-cost materials as we head into winter:.

    It has been revealed that bubble wrap is so useful when winterizing your garden and, covered with a layer of burlap, looks pretty smart. I like to tie red ribbon around for the holidays, too, and my winter protection looks like Christmas decor! Re-using materials in your garden, whether you're recycling cardboard as a mulch or trying a few DIY upcycling projects to upgrade your garden storage, makes your garden budget go further, too.
